source.title: Capacity-Aware Mixture Law Enables Efficient LLM Data Optimization
source.authors: Jingwei Li; Xin-Ran Gu; Jingzhao Zhang

record.file_problem: None noted; the supplied paper text includes the main sections and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests validation-loss extrapolation across model scales and validation-loss-to-benchmark prediction using a capacity-aware mixture law, rather than reproducing the original parameter/token/compute scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper studies data-mixture-dependent validation loss and downstream benchmark prediction. It does not sweep parameter count, training tokens, and compute to test the original laws or the compute-optimal parameter/token split. Table 1 and Table 2 report realized benchmark scores for mixture-selection methods, not direct prediction errors for the loss-to-benchmark mapping; those scores are not cataloged as rows here. Figure 3's domain training-loss ratios are included as related findings, but they are not held-out loss results.
record.test_reason: The study fits a size-dependent power-law mixture law (CAMEL) on smaller MoE models during a mid-training cooldown and checks held-out-scale validation-loss extrapolation, which bears on V1 and V2. It also fits a multi-loss logistic mapping from validation losses to benchmark accuracy on held-out checkpoints, which bears on V6. This is a new setting (data-mixture cooldown) rather than a parameter/token/compute sweep. The V6 result is the only one with a readable outcome. The loss-extrapolation results are reported only as relative comparisons in figures.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that CAMEL, a size-and-mixture-coupled law, gives lower validation-loss extrapolation error than DML/SODM. They conclude that a multi-loss logistic mapping predicts benchmark accuracy well and that Hourglass sampling beats uniform allocation under a fixed budget. They also report that mixtures chosen for the 55B-A1.2B target give the highest weighted benchmark scores, with at least 50% less optimization compute and up to 3% better benchmarks.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a capacity-aware, data-mixture-dependent validation-loss law and a loss-to-benchmark mapping. It does not reproduce Kaplan et al.'s parameter/token/compute sweeps or Hoffmann et al.'s compute-optimal parameter-token allocation; models use a pretraining stage followed by a 20B-token cooldown with varied mixtures.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction error varies with the sampling strategy for fitting points; Hourglass is reported to have the lowest error. The intrinsic-domain ablation reports minimum error around k=5, with higher error for too-small or too-large k. The number of sampled training points and the mixture/model-scale configurations also vary across the prediction experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-domain training-loss reductions with model size differ (R_math≈2.4 vs R_know≈4.3 at step 2000). Authors read this as non-proportional capacity allocation across domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss on different data domains improves at different rates as model size grows.

fits_no_version.finding: The choice of fitting-point allocation across scales (Hourglass vs Rectangle, Triangle, Inverted Triangle, Diamond) changes the extrapolation error of the mixture law under fixed compute. The number of intrinsic domains k also matters, with minimum error near k=5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The extrapolation accuracy of mixture scaling laws depends on experiment-design and fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: CAMEL-derived optimal mixtures shift toward Knowledge data and away from Math/Code as model size grows (Figure 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-optimal data mixtures change systematically with model scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Numerical error values for the validation-loss and benchmark-accuracy prediction plots are not provided in the text; prediction results are largely shown as figures. The paper gives inconsistent target-scale descriptions: the main text describes evaluation on a 55B-A1.2B model, while Appendix C.1 describes extrapolation and evaluation at M=20. The reported held-out model-scale validation-loss test is M=12 and does not establish extrapolation over several orders of magnitude.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numeric rows for Table 1 or Table 2: these are realized benchmark scores for mixture-selection methods, not direct measurements of the claim's loss-scaling or loss-to-accuracy prediction error. The Figure 10 intrinsic-domain-count ablation is summarized under method_sensitivity because the text gives no numeric error values and it does not directly measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No readable test of power-law form. The size range is about one order of magnitude in activated parameters (A12M–A150M, M=4–12). Validation loss is measured after a 20B-token cooldown, not as pretraining-loss curves. Tokens and compute are not varied.
Extrapolation is from M≤10 to M=12 only, with no absolute error readable. The M=20 (55B-A1.2B) target is evaluated only through benchmark scores of the chosen mixtures, not through loss prediction.
Not tested; depth and width are tied to M.
Extrapolation of the loss-to-accuracy mapping to a larger held-out scale is not tested. Monotonic improvement of benchmarks with scale is not reported.
Published exponents and compute-optimal splits are not compared.

missing.what: Optimal mixture weights as a function of model size (Knowledge share rises; Math and Code fall)

record.verdict_notes: CAMEL assumes a per-domain power law in effective parameters, and its loss term has the form K_i/(<t_i,r>^α M^β). The study therefore builds on V1 rather than independently testing it, and the only loss-extrapolation evidence is relative to other mixture laws and figure-only. No verdict is given on V1 or V2 for that reason. The scale descriptions are inconsistent: eight scales are described, the fit range is stated as 590M-A12M to 7B-A150M, the held-out test is M=12 in Appendix B.1, and the target is M=20 / 55B-A1.2B in Appendix C.1. It is unclear whether M=12 lies inside the stated fit range. The downstream benchmark results in Tables 1 and 2 compare mixture-selection methods and do not test V6 prediction accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation-loss prediction as model scale and data mixture vary. Does not test independent parameter-, token-, and compute-scaling laws with the other quantities non-bottlenecked, or establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.

Tests extrapolation from smaller model scales to held-out scale M=12 for validation loss, and evaluates benchmark prediction on held-out checkpoints. Does not demonstrate prediction across orders of magnitude.
No fixed training-compute sweep that finds loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Does not test whether the same law holds in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer. The paper's mid-training mixture setting is not a test of those stated cases.

Tests validation-loss prediction of benchmark accuracy across checkpoints and benchmarks. Does not test a general downstream performance scaling law across orders of magnitude or establish that benchmark performance improves monotonically with scale.

Compares mixture-law formulations and sampling strategies for prediction error, but does not test whether published parameter/token/compute exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with setup, nor whether those loss curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Deepseek V3 architecture model family (CAMEL)
rows.size_stated: Training scales M ∈ {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10}; held-out test scale M=12. The paper also describes fit models from 590M-A12M to 7B-A150M.
rows.stage_stated: Mid-training; models are pretrained to estimated compute-optimal tokens, then trained for an additional 20B tokens during cooldown with varied mixtures.
rows.operation_detail: Fit CAMEL validation-loss mixture law on smaller scales and evaluate validation-loss prediction at a held-out model scale.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over 20 repetitions; uncertainty statistic not stated
rows.note: The authors state CAMEL consistently outperforms the baselines across different training samples and has more stable extrapolation. The plotted error values are not given in text.
rows.check: Error values are figure-only. The text says only that CAMEL has lower error and is 'more stable' than DML/SODM, which is a relative comparison of the study's own method against baselines. There is no absolute extrapolation accuracy and no fitted exponent, so it cannot show whether the power law holds or extrapolates well. The extrapolation is also short: fit on M≤10, test on M=12.
